A test is only worth adding if it actually fails when the behavior it covers is broken. Several reviews caught tests that looked correct but could never fail: an assertion chain like `value.should.deepEqual(...)` silently short-circuits when `value` is `undefined`, so a dropped field goes undetected — fix by asserting on the wrapped value instead, e.g. `should(value).deepEqual(...)`. A plural-key check that stripped all CLDR suffixes before comparing passed even when a locale was missing required forms; it had to require the exact set of cardinal categories per locale to mean anything. A fixture where every "overloaded" test case also contained the word "overloaded" in the message meant the error-code check was never actually exercised on its own — the fix split cases so each one isolates the single condition it claims to test (e.g. a known capacity code with a neutral message, and an unknown code with a neutral message that must stay non-retryable). An async test asserted a waiter resolved, but the waiter was created after the condition it waited on had already been satisfied, so it couldn't fail on a real regression — the fix reordered the test to start waiting before the condition occurs. A removed cap and a cursor/skip fix were both validated by confirming the regression test fails on the old code and passes on the new one.

When writing or reviewing a test, actively check two things: (1) does the assertion genuinely fail if the implementation is wrong (not just syntactically present but logically capable of failing — watch for optional chaining, loose matchers, or overly permissive normalization in test helpers), and (2) does the fixture isolate the one thing being tested, without other factors (shared substrings, confounded flags, pre-satisfied conditions) accidentally making the assertion pass regardless of the code under test. Where feasible, confirm this directly — revert the fix (or mutate the implementation) and verify the test fails, or use property-based/fuzz testing for stateful sequences where a single example is unlikely to find ordering bugs.
